references.text: Jesus' parallel teaching in the Sermon on the Mount about reconciling with one's opponent quickly, before being handed over to the judge and thrown into prison ([ref:Matt 5:25-26|Matthew 5:25-26]). This is the closest parallel to Luke 12:58-59 and contains almost identical wording and message.

Proverbs urges not to rush to court, but rather to resolve the matter directly with one's opponent: "Do not go hastily to court" ([ref:Ordsp 25:8|Proverbs 25:8]). This reflects the same wisdom about making things right with your opponent before the case ends up before a judge.
The continuation of the exhortation in Proverbs to settle disputes directly with one's neighbor, to avoid shame and lasting consequences ([ref:Ordsp 25:9-10|Proverbs 25:9-10]).

In the parable of the unforgiving servant, the one who does not forgive is handed over to the jailers until the entire debt is paid ([ref:Matt 18:34-35|Matthew 18:34-35]). This shares the motif of being handed over and imprisoned until the debt is settled.

Isaiah urges seeking the Lord while he may be found, and calling on him while he is near ([ref:Jes 55:6-7|Isaiah 55:6-7]). Luke 12:58 speaks of making things right in time, which in the spiritual context points to seeking reconciliation with God while there is still time.

The preceding verse where Jesus encourages his listeners to judge for themselves what is right ([ref:Luk 12:57|Luke 12:57]), and which forms the immediate context for the illustration about reconciling with one's opponent on the way to the authorities.

The following verse that completes the illustration with the warning that one will not be released until the last penny is paid ([ref:Luk 12:59|Luke 12:59]), and underscores the seriousness of not making things right in time.
